sentences.t: Bēowulf maþelode, bearn Ecgþēowes:
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words, child of Ecgtheow:
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words, the son of Ecgtheow:
sentences.n: ‘maþelode’ is the house formula for a formal speech (‘spoke in speech-words’), and ‘bearn Ecgþēowes’, ‘child of Ecgtheow’, stands in apposition to the name. The colon tells us the speech follows at once, and the opening quotation mark in the next line is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
‘Hwæt, wē þē þās sǣlāc, sunu Healfdenes,
lēod Scyldinga, lustum brōhton
tīres tō tācne, þē þū hēr tō lōcast.
sentences.l: ‘What! We gladly brought to you this sea-gift, son of Healfdene, prince of the Scyldings, as a token of glory, which you look at here.
sentences.i: ‘Listen! We have gladly brought you this gift from the sea, son of Healfdene, prince of the Scyldings, as a token of glory; you are looking at it here.
sentences.n: ‘Hwæt’ is the house ‘What!’ (‘Listen!’). ‘wē … brōhton’ is ‘we brought’, with ‘þē’ the dative ‘to you’ and ‘þās sǣlāc’ the object. ‘sǣlāc’ is ‘sea-gift’ (‘sǣ’ ‘sea’ and ‘lāc’ ‘gift’, also ‘play’), the same word as ‘sǣlāce’ at 1624, here the head and the hilt Beowulf has carried up from the mere. ‘sunu Healfdenes’ and ‘lēod Scyldinga’ (‘prince of the Scyldings’) both name Hrothgar. ‘lustum’ is a dative plural, ‘with pleasures, gladly’. ‘tīres tō tācne’ is ‘as a token of glory’, ‘tīres’ a genitive and ‘tācne’ a dative after ‘tō’. The second ‘þē’ is the relative word ‘which’, and ‘þū hēr tō lōcast’ is ‘you look at here’, ‘lōcian’ taking ‘tō’ for what is looked at.

sentences.l: I came through that with difficulty with my life, in battle under the water; I ventured the work laboriously;
sentences.i: I barely came out alive from that fight under the water; I dared the deed at great cost;
sentences.n: ‘gedīgde’ is the past of ‘gedīgan’, ‘come through, survive’, with ‘þæt’ its object and ‘ealdre’ a dative, ‘with my life’. ‘unsōfte’ is ‘not softly, with difficulty’. ‘wigge’ is a dative, ‘in battle’; the apparatus records Thorpe’s ‘weorce’ and the reading ‘wīg and weorce’, and says that many editors read the two lines as one clause, ‘in battle under the water I ventured the work with difficulty’. ‘genēþde’ is the past of ‘genēþan’, ‘venture, dare’, with ‘weorc’ its object. Klaeber’s semicolon after ‘earfoðlīce’ sets off what comes next.

sentences.t:
ætrihte wæs
gūð getwǣfed, nymðe mec God scylde.
sentences.l: almost the strife was broken off, unless God had shielded me.
sentences.i: the fight was all but broken off for me, had God not shielded me.
sentences.n: ‘ætrihte’ is ‘almost, all but’. ‘getwǣfed’ is the past participle of ‘getwǣfan’, ‘part, cut off, put an end to’, and with ‘gūð’ as subject Klaeber reads ‘the fight was all but ended’, the end being Beowulf’s loss. The apparatus records Grein, Bugge, Trautmann and Sedgefield, who read ‘gūðe’, a dative, and take ‘wæs’ as ‘I was’: ‘I was all but parted from the fight’, which comes to the same danger. ‘nymðe mec God scylde’ is ‘unless God shielded me’, with ‘nymðe’ ‘unless’ and the past subjunctive ‘scylde’; ‘mec’ is an older form of ‘mē’.

sentences.t:
Ne meahte ic æt hilde mid Hruntinge
wiht gewyrcan, þēah þæt wǣpen duge;
sentences.l: I could do nothing at the fight with Hrunting, though that weapon is good;
sentences.i: At the fight I could do nothing with Hrunting, good as that weapon is;
sentences.n: ‘wiht gewyrcan’ is ‘accomplish anything’, ‘wiht’ the object of the infinitive. ‘Hruntinge’ is the dative of the sword’s name, left untranslated. It was Unferth’s sword, lent for the dive, and it would not bite the mere-woman (1455–1472 and 1519–1528). ‘þēah þæt wǣpen duge’ is ‘though that weapon avails’: ‘duge’ is a present subjunctive of ‘dugan’, ‘be good, avail’, the mood that goes with ‘þēah’ for a granted point.

sentences.t:
ac mē geūðe ylda Waldend,
þæt ic on wāge geseah wlitig hangian
ealdsweord ēacen — oftost wīsode
winigea lēasum —, þæt ic ðȳ wǣpne gebrǣd.
sentences.l: but the Wielder of men granted me that I saw hanging on the wall a beautiful old sword, huge — most often he guided the friendless — so that I drew that weapon.
sentences.i: but the Ruler of men granted me to see a beautiful old sword of giant size hanging on the wall — he most often guided the friendless — and I drew that weapon.
sentences.n: ‘geūðe’ is the past of ‘geunnan’, ‘grant’, with the dative ‘mē’ for the person and a ‘þæt’ clause for the gift. ‘ylda Waldend’ is ‘Wielder of men’ (‘ylda’ a genitive plural, ‘men, mankind’), the ‘Wielder’ of fitt 02 (‘wuldres Waldend’, ‘glory’s Wielder’), where the idiomatic line says ‘Ruler’. ‘on wāge’ is ‘on the wall’. The apparatus marks a new manuscript leaf (fol. 166b) at ‘hangian’, and credits the word to Thorkelin’s transcript A. ‘ealdsweord’ and ‘ēacen’ (‘huge’) are the old sword of the last fitt (1558); the apparatus refers to 1558a, where editors print it as two words. The dashes set off ‘oftost wīsode winigea lēasum’, ‘most often he guided those lacking friends’: ‘winigea’ is a genitive plural, ‘of friends’, depending on ‘lēasum’, a dative plural, ‘to the friendless’. ‘Waldend’ is the unstated subject, so the aside says that God most often shows the friendless the way; the apparatus lists Sievers, Holthausen and Sedgefield, who read ‘oft’ for ‘oftost’. ‘ðȳ wǣpne’ is an instrumental or dative, and ‘gebrǣd’ the past of ‘gebregdan’, ‘draw, snatch’; I take ‘I drew that weapon’, a rendering that fits the plain sense but is a guess at the exact case relation.

sentences.t:
Ofslōh ðā æt þǣre sæcce, þā mē sǣl āgeald,
hūses hyrdas.
sentences.l: Then at that strife I slew the keepers of the house, when the occasion paid out to me.
sentences.i: Then in that struggle I killed the guardians of the house, when the chance was given me.
sentences.n: ‘Ofslōh’ has no stated subject; it is ‘ic’, Beowulf. ‘ðā’ is ‘then’, and ‘æt þǣre sæcce’ ‘at that strife’. ‘þā mē sǣl āgeald’ is ‘when the occasion paid out to me’: ‘āgeald’ is the past of ‘āgildan’, ‘pay out, repay’, with ‘sǣl’ (‘occasion, favourable time’) as subject and ‘mē’ a dative, so ‘when the chance came to me’. ‘hūses hyrdas’ is ‘keepers of the house’, a plural although the mother alone was killed there; the text does not say whom the plural takes in, and Beowulf may be speaking loosely of the pair, Grendel having been dead before.

sentences.t:
Þā þæt hildebil
forbarn brogdenmǣl, swā þæt blōd gesprang,
hātost heaþoswāta.
sentences.l: Then that battle-blade, the braided-marked one, burned up, so that the blood sprang forth, hottest of battle-sweats.
sentences.i: Then that war-blade, the patterned sword, burned away, so that the blood sprang out, the hottest blood of battle.
sentences.n: ‘hildebil’ is ‘battle-blade’, the giant sword, ‘forbarn’ the past of ‘forbeornan’, ‘burn up’, and ‘brogdenmǣl’ the ‘braided-marked’ blade of 1616, where Klaeber prints ‘brōdenmǣl’; this form has the ‘g’ of the participle ‘brogden’, ‘woven’, from ‘bregdan’. ‘swā þæt’ introduces the result, ‘so that’, and ‘gesprang’ is the past of ‘gespringan’, ‘spring forth’. ‘hātost heaþoswāta’ is a superlative with a partitive genitive plural, ‘hottest of battle-sweats’: ‘heaþoswāt’ is the house ‘battle-sweat’ for the blood of a fight (1460, 1606), here the poisonous blood that melted the blade. Beowulf tells the hall what the reader saw at 1605–1617.

sentences.t:
Ic þæt hilt þanan
fēondum ætferede;
sentences.l: I carried that hilt away from there from the foes;
sentences.i: I carried the hilt away from there, out of my foes’ hands;
sentences.n: ‘þanan’ is ‘from there’. ‘ætferede’ is the past of ‘ætferian’, ‘carry away, take from’, and ‘fēondum’ a dative, ‘from the foes’. ‘Ic’ is the subject, ‘þæt hilt’ the object; ‘hilt’ is neuter here, with ‘þæt’. The semicolon sets off the next clause, which says what else he did.

sentences.t:
fyrendǣda wræc,
dēaðcwealm Denigea, swā hit gedēfe wæs.
sentences.l: I avenged the crimes, the death-slaughter of the Danes, as it was fitting.
sentences.i: I took vengeance for the crimes, the slaughter of the Danes, as was right.
sentences.n: ‘wræc’ is the past of ‘wrecan’, ‘avenge’, with unstated ‘ic’. ‘fyrendǣda’ is a genitive plural of ‘fyrendǣd’, ‘crime’ (‘fyren’ ‘sin, crime’, as in ‘fyrena hyrde’), and I take it as depending on ‘wræc’; it could instead be an accusative plural with ‘dēaðcwealm Denigea’ in apposition, which gives the same sense. ‘dēaðcwealm’ is ‘death-slaughter’ and ‘Denigea’ the genitive plural of ‘Dene’, ‘of the Danes’. ‘swā hit gedēfe wæs’ is ‘as it was fitting’, ‘gedēfe’ ‘suitable, proper’.

sentences.t:
Ic hit þē þonne gehāte, þæt þū on Heorote mōst
sorhlēas swefan mid þīnra secga gedryht,
ond þegna gehwylc þīnra lēoda,
duguðe ond iogoþe, þæt þū him ondrǣdan ne þearft,
þēoden Scyldinga, on þā healfe,
aldọrbealu eorlum, swā þū ǣr dydest.’
sentences.l: I promise it to you then, that you may sleep free of sorrow in Heorot with the troop of your men, and each of the thanes of your people, of the proven and the young, that you need not fear for them, prince of the Scyldings, on that side, life-bale for the earls, as you did before.’
sentences.i: So I promise you that you may sleep free of care in Heorot with your company of men, and every thane of your people, old hands and young, and that you need not fear for them, prince of the Scyldings, any deadly harm to your earls from that side, as you did before.’
sentences.n: ‘Ic hit þē þonne gehāte’ is ‘I then promise it to you’, ‘gehāte’ a first-person present of ‘gehātan’, ‘promise’, and ‘þonne’ ‘then, in that case’. ‘þæt þū … mōst’ is ‘that you may’, ‘mōst’ the second-person present of ‘mōtan’, ‘be allowed, may’ (the indicative form; the permission is stated as a fact), with ‘swefan’ ‘sleep’ and ‘sorhlēas’ ‘free of sorrow’. ‘mid þīnra secga gedryht’ is ‘with the troop of your men’. ‘ond þegna gehwylc’ is ‘and each of the thanes’, a second subject of the same clause, with ‘duguðe ond iogoþe’ (‘of the proven warriors and the young’) in apposition. The second ‘þæt’ clause gives the result: ‘þæt þū him ondrǣdan ne þearft’ is ‘that you need not dread for them’, ‘him’ a dative plural, ‘þearft’ the second person of ‘þurfan’, ‘need’, and the object, ‘aldọrbealu eorlum’, is ‘life-bale to the earls’, harm that kills; ‘on þā healfe’ is ‘on that side’, from Grendel’s kin. The dot under the ‘ọ’ in ‘aldọrbealu’ is Klaeber’s sign that this vowel does not count in the metre; the word is scanned as if the vowel were not there. ‘swā þū ǣr dydest’ is ‘as you did before’: the Danes have feared for their lives since Grendel first came. The closing quotation mark ends Beowulf’s speech.

sentences.l: Then was the golden hilt given into the hand of the old warrior, the hoary battle-leader, the ancient work of giants;
sentences.i: Then the golden hilt was given into the hand of the old warrior, the grey-haired leader in battle, the ancient work of giants;
sentences.n: ‘wæs … gyfen’ is a passive, ‘was given’, with ‘gylden hilt’ the subject and ‘on hand’ ‘into the hand’. ‘gamelum rince’ (‘to the old warrior’) and ‘hārum hildfruman’ (‘to the hoary battle-leader’) are datives naming Hrothgar; ‘hildfruma’ is ‘battle-first, battle-leader’ (‘fruma’ ‘first, chief’). ‘enta ǣrgeweorc’ is ‘ancient work of giants’, ‘enta’ a genitive plural of ‘ent’, ‘giant’, and ‘ǣrgeweorc’ ‘work of former times’. The apparatus records Kluge and Holthausen, who print ‘gylden hilt’ as one word, ‘Gyldenhilt’, a name for the sword (Klaeber’s Introduction, p. xviii, note).

sentences.l: it passed into the possession of the lord of the Danes, after the fall of devils, the work of wonder-smiths;
sentences.i: it passed into the possession of the Danes’ lord after the fall of the fiends, a work of wonder-smiths;
sentences.n: ‘hit’ is the hilt. ‘on ǣht gehwearf’ is ‘passed into possession’, ‘gehwearf’ the past of ‘gehweorfan’, ‘turn, pass’, and ‘Denigea freân’ is ‘to the lord of the Danes’, a dative, Hrothgar (the circumflex of ‘freân’ is Klaeber’s mark, placed on the second vowel). ‘æfter dēofla hryre’ is ‘after the fall of devils’: ‘dēofol’ is the Christian ‘devil’, used of Grendel and his mother as at 756, and I take ‘hryre’ to be their fall; it could instead mean the destruction of the giants, whom the next lines call the Flood’s victims, and the text does not decide it. ‘wundọrsmiþa geweorc’ is ‘work of wonder-smiths’ (‘wundor’ ‘wonder’ and ‘smiþ’ ‘smith’), the giants as makers, in apposition to ‘hit’. The dot under the ‘ọ’ is the same metrical sign as in ‘aldọrbealu’ at 1676.

sentences.l: and when the grim-hearted man, God’s adversary, guilty of murder, gave up this world, and his mother too;
sentences.i: and when the grim-hearted man, God’s enemy, guilty of murder, left this world, and his mother too;
sentences.n: ‘ond þā’ is ‘and when’, with ‘þā’ a conjunction; the apparatus records Müllenhoff, Holthausen and Sedgefield, who drop ‘ond’. ‘ofgeaf’ is the past of ‘ofgiefan’, ‘give up, leave’, the verb of 1600 (‘ofgēafon’), with ‘þās worold’ the object. The subject is ‘gromheort guma’ (‘grim-hearted man’), Grendel, ‘Godes andsaca’ the house ‘God’s adversary’ in apposition, and ‘morðres scyldig’ ‘guilty of murder’, ‘scyldig’ taking the genitive. ‘ond his mōdor ēac’ adds a second subject after the verb, ‘and his mother too’, and the singular verb agrees with the first.

sentences.t:
on geweald gehwearf woroldcyninga
ðǣm sēlestan be sǣm twēonum
ðāra þe on Scedenigge sceattas dǣlde.
sentences.l: it passed into the power of the best of world-kings between the seas, of those who in Scedenig dealt out treasures.
sentences.i: it passed into the power of the best of the world’s kings between the seas, of all who ever dealt out treasure in Scedenig.
sentences.n: ‘on geweald gehwearf’ is ‘passed into the power of’, with ‘ðǣm sēlestan’ (‘the best’) a dative and ‘woroldcyninga’ a genitive plural, ‘of world-kings’. ‘be sǣm twēonum’ is ‘between the seas’, an old phrase with ‘twēonum’ the dative plural of ‘twēon’, literally ‘between the two’; the apparatus marks a new manuscript leaf (fol. 167a) at ‘sæm’. ‘ðāra þe … dǣlde’ is ‘of those who dealt out’, with a singular verb after a plural, and ‘sceattas’ is ‘treasures’ (originally ‘coins’). ‘Scedenigge’ is the dative of ‘Scedenig’, ‘Scania’, the south of Scandinavia, the land of ‘Scedelandum’ at 19; the apparatus says the manuscript’s first ‘g’ was written over an ‘n’. Giving out treasure is the mark of a good king, so Hrothgar is called the best of them.

sentences.l: Hrothgar spoke in speech-words — he looked at the hilt, the old relic, on which was written the origin of ancient strife;
sentences.i: Hrothgar spoke in formal words — he was examining the hilt, that old relic, on which was written the beginning of the ancient strife;
sentences.n: ‘maðelode’ is the same verb as ‘maþelode’, with ‘ð’ for ‘þ’, and the house rendering is the same. The dash cuts the formula off: the speech itself begins only at 1700, after the poet has Hrothgar look at the hilt. ‘hylt scēawode’ is ‘looked at the hilt’, ‘hylt’ a spelling of ‘hilt’, and ‘ealde lāfe’ ‘old legacy, relic’ (‘lāf’ ‘what is left’). ‘on ðǣm wæs ōr writen fyrngewinnes’ is ‘on which was written the origin of ancient strife’: ‘ōr’ is ‘beginning’, ‘writen’ ‘written, engraved’, and ‘fyrngewinn’ ‘ancient strife’ (‘fyrn’ ‘old’ and ‘gewinn’ ‘struggle’), the war of the giants against God that follows.

sentences.l: when the flood, the pouring ocean, slew the race of giants — they fared dreadfully;
sentences.i: when the flood, the pouring sea, destroyed the race of giants — they came to a dreadful end;
sentences.n: ‘syðþan’ is ‘when’ or ‘after’, and ‘flōd’ the subject of ‘ofslōh’, ‘slew’. ‘gifen gēotende’ is ‘pouring ocean’: ‘gifen’ is a noun for the ocean, ‘gēotende’ the present participle of ‘gēotan’, ‘pour’, and the pair is in apposition to ‘flōd’. ‘gīganta cyn’ is ‘the race of giants’, the object. ‘frēcne gefērdon’ is a guess: ‘gefēran’ can mean ‘go through, bring about’, and ‘frēcne’ ‘dreadfully, boldly’, so the clause is either ‘they fared dreadfully’, which I follow, or ‘they had dared terrible things’. The giants’ war against God and the reward God paid them are told at 113–114; the Flood itself is told here.

sentences.t:
þæt wæs fremde þēod
ēcean Dryhtne;
sentences.l: that was a people alien to the eternal Lord;
sentences.i: that was a people estranged from the eternal Lord;
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ is a neuter pronoun for the people, ‘fremde’ is ‘foreign, estranged’, and ‘ēcean Dryhtne’ is a dative, ‘to the eternal Lord’ (‘ēcean’ the weak form of ‘ēce’, ‘eternal’). So the giants were cut off from God, as the descendants of Cain, whom the poet names with the giants at 111–114.

sentences.t:
him þæs endelēan
þurh wæteres wylm Waldend sealde.
sentences.l: to them for that the Wielder gave final reward through the surge of water.
sentences.i: For that the Wielder gave them their final reward through the surging of the water.
sentences.n: ‘him’ is a dative plural, ‘to them’, and ‘þæs’ a genitive, ‘for that’; ‘endelēan’ is ‘final reward’, a compound of ‘ende’ and ‘lēan’, in the sense of requital. The pattern is that of 114, where God paid the giants ‘lēan’ for their war, and of 1584, where Beowulf paid Grendel ‘lēan’ for the raids. ‘þurh wæteres wylm’ is ‘through the surge of water’, and ‘Waldend’ the ‘Wielder’ again, as at 1661.

sentences.t:
Swā wæs on ðǣm scennum scīran goldes
þurh rūnstafas rihte gemearcod,
geseted ond gesǣd, hwām þæt sweord geworht,
īrena cyst ǣrest wǣre,
wreoþenhilt ond wyrmfāh.
sentences.l: So was marked rightly through rune-staves on the plates of bright gold, set down and said, for whom that sword was first made, the choicest of irons, with twisted hilt and serpent-patterned.
sentences.i: So on the plates of bright gold it was rightly marked in runic letters, set down and told, for whom that sword was first made, the finest of blades, with its twisted hilt and its pattern of serpents.
sentences.n: ‘Swā wæs … gemearcod’ is ‘so it was marked’, ‘gemearcod’ the past participle of ‘gemearcian’, ‘mark, engrave’, with ‘scīran goldes’ ‘of bright gold’ and ‘on ðǣm scennum’ ‘on the plates’, a dative plural; ‘scenn’ is a rare word and I read it as ‘plate’, a guess. ‘rūnstafas’ are ‘rune-staves’, letters. ‘rihte’ is ‘rightly, exactly’. ‘geseted ond gesǣd’ is ‘set down and said’. ‘hwām þæt sweord geworht … wǣre’ is an indirect question in the subjunctive, ‘for whom that sword had been made’, with ‘ǣrest’ ‘first’ and ‘īrena cyst’ ‘choicest of irons’, as at 673, where the apparatus gives variant readings (it refers to 673a). ‘wreoþenhilt’ is ‘twisted-hilt’ (‘wreoþen’ the participle of ‘wrīðan’, ‘twist’) and ‘wyrmfāh’ ‘serpent-patterned’ (‘wyrm’ ‘snake, dragon’ and ‘fāh’ ‘coloured’), two adjectives used of the sword; the sense of ‘wyrmfāh’ may be a snake-like pattern on the blade or on the hilt, and I cannot say which.

sentences.t:
Ðā se wīsa spræc
sunu Healfdenes — swīgedon ealle —:
sentences.l: Then the wise one spoke, the son of Healfdene — all were silent —:
sentences.i: Then the wise king spoke, Healfdene’s son — and all kept silent —:
sentences.n: ‘se wīsa’ is ‘the wise one’, an adjective with the definite article used as a noun, and ‘sunu Healfdenes’ stands in apposition. ‘swīgedon ealle’ is ‘all were silent’, a plural past of ‘swīgian’, set off by dashes as a side remark. The colon opens Hrothgar’s speech, which runs to the end of this part and beyond.

sentences.t:
‘Þæt, lā, mæg secgan sē þe sōð ond riht
fremeð on folce, feor eal gemon,
eald ēþelweard, þæt ðes eorl wǣre
geboren betera!
sentences.l: ‘That, lo, may he say who does truth and right among the people, who remembers everything far back, the old guardian of the homeland, that this earl was born better!
sentences.i: ‘Anyone who does truth and right among his people, and remembers everything far back, an old guardian of his homeland, may say this: that this earl was born the better man!
sentences.n: ‘Þæt’ is the object of ‘secgan’ and is resolved by the ‘þæt’ clause at the end. ‘lā’ is ‘lo’. ‘sē þe sōð ond riht fremeð on folce’ is ‘he who does truth and right among the people’, and ‘feor eal gemon’ is ‘remembers all of it from far back’ (‘gemon’ a present of ‘gemunan’), with ‘eald ēþelweard’ (‘old guardian of the homeland’) in apposition. The apparatus says the manuscript has a rune, the one named ‘ēþel’ (‘homeland’), in place of the word; Klaeber spells it out. ‘þæt ðes eorl wǣre geboren betera’ is ‘that this earl was born better’, ‘betera’ a comparative with no stated comparison, ‘better than others’. Bugge and Trautmann read ‘þæt ðē eorl nǣre’, ‘that no earl was born better than you’ (the apparatus refers to Klaeber’s notes on the Language, § 25.2, and at 1850). The description fits the speaker, Hrothgar, an old guardian of his homeland.

sentences.t:
Blǣd is ārǣred
geond wīdwegas, wine mīn Bēowulf,
ðīn ofer þēoda gehwylce.
sentences.l: Glory is raised up through the far ways, friend mine Beowulf, yours over every people.
sentences.i: Your glory, my friend Beowulf, is raised up throughout the wide world, over every people.
sentences.n: ‘Blǣd’ is ‘glory, prosperity’ and ‘ārǣred’ the past participle of ‘ārǣran’, ‘raise up’. ‘geond wīdwegas’ is ‘through the wide ways’, that is, far lands. ‘wine mīn Bēowulf’ is the house ‘friend mine Beowulf’ of 457 (and 530, where it is said to Unferth). ‘ðīn’ is placed after the verb for emphasis, ‘yours’, with ‘ofer þēoda gehwylce’ ‘over every people’.

sentences.t:
Eal þū hit geþyldum healdest,
mægen mid mōdes snyttrum.
sentences.l: You hold it all with patience, might with wisdom of mind.
sentences.i: You hold it all with steadiness, your strength joined to a wise mind.
sentences.n: ‘hit’ is the glory just named, or more loosely ‘all of it’; the text does not say. ‘geþyldum’ is a dative plural of ‘geþyld’, ‘patience, steadiness’, and ‘healdest’ the second person of ‘healdan’, ‘hold, keep’. ‘mægen mid mōdes snyttrum’ is ‘might with wisdom of mind’, ‘snyttrum’ a dative plural of ‘snyttru’, ‘wisdom’.

sentences.t:
Ic þē sceal mīne gelǣstan
frēode, swā wit furðum sprǣcon.
sentences.l: I shall fulfil to you my friendship, as we two spoke just now.
sentences.i: I shall make good my friendship to you, as we two spoke a little while ago.
sentences.n: ‘sceal … gelǣstan’ is ‘shall fulfil’, ‘gelǣstan’ ‘perform, carry out’, and ‘mīne frēode’ its object, ‘my friendship’, an accusative singular. The apparatus records the manuscript readings ‘freode’ and ‘freoðe’ (the latter would be ‘protection’), and Klaeber prints ‘frēode’. ‘wit’ is the dual pronoun, ‘we two’, ‘furðum’ ‘just now, lately’, and ‘sprǣcon’ the plural past of ‘sprecan’. The text does not say which exchange this means; the nearest is the talk between the two before the dive.

sentences.t:
Ðū scealt tō frōfre weorþan
eal langtwīdig lēodum þīnum,
hæleðum tō helpe.
sentences.l: You shall become for comfort, all long-lasting, to your people, to heroes for help.
sentences.i: You shall be a comfort to your people, lasting all your days, a help to your heroes.
sentences.n: ‘tō frōfre weorþan’ is ‘become a comfort’, ‘weorþan’ ‘become’. ‘eal langtwīdig’ is ‘wholly long-lasting’; ‘langtwīdig’ is a word the lexica record only here, and I take it to mean ‘lasting a long time’, which is a guess from the parts. ‘lēodum þīnum’ and ‘hæleðum’ are datives, ‘to your people’ and ‘to heroes’, and ‘tō helpe’ ‘for help’. The apparatus marks a new manuscript leaf (fol. 167b) at ‘hæleðum’, where the word is read from the Thorkelin transcripts, B and A.

sentences.t:
Ne wearð Heremōd swā
eaforum Ecgwelan, Ār-Scyldingum;
sentences.l: Not so did Heremod become to the sons of Ecgwela, the Ār-Scyldings;
sentences.i: Heremod was not so to the sons of Ecgwela, the Ār-Scyldings;
sentences.n: ‘Ne wearð Heremōd swā’ is ‘Heremod did not become so’, ‘wearð’ the past of ‘weorþan’ and ‘swā’ ‘in that way’, as you will be. Heremod is the Danish king set beside Sigemund at 901 as one who began well and went wrong. ‘eaforum Ecgwelan’ is a dative plural, ‘to the descendants of Ecgwela’, Ecgwela being an early Danish king named only here; ‘Ār-Scyldingum’ is the dative of ‘Ār-Scyldingas’, left untranslated as a name for the Danes (‘ār’ is probably ‘honour, grace’, a guess), the Danes once more. The apparatus records Schaldemose, Holtzmann and Müllenhoff, who print the singular ‘eafora’, so that Heremod himself is ‘the descendant of Ecgwela’: ‘Heremod, Ecgwela’s offspring, did not become so to the Honour-Scyldings’.

sentences.t:
ne gewēox hē him tō willan, ac tō wælfealle
ond tō dēaðcwalum Deniga lēodum;
sentences.l: he did not grow up to their pleasure, but to slaughter-fall and to death-pangs for the people of the Danes;
sentences.i: he did not grow up to please them, but to bring slaughter and death on the people of the Danes;
sentences.n: ‘gewēox’ is the past of ‘gewexan’, ‘grow up’, and ‘him tō willan’ is ‘to their will, to their pleasure’. ‘ac tō wælfealle ond tō dēaðcwalum’ is ‘but to slaughter-fall and death-agonies’: ‘wælfeall’ is a fall in slaughter, and ‘dēaðcwalu’ (plural ‘dēaðcwalum’) ‘death-pang, violent death’. ‘Deniga lēodum’ is ‘to the people of the Danes’, a dative.

sentences.t:
brēat bolgenmōd bēodgenēatas,
eaxlgesteallan, oþ þæt hē āna hwearf,
mǣre þēoden mondrēamum from.
sentences.l: swollen-minded, he broke the table-companions, the shoulder-companions, until he alone turned away, the famed lord, away from the joys of men.
sentences.i: In a swollen rage he cut down his table-companions, the comrades at his shoulder, until he went off alone, that famed prince, away from the joys of men.
sentences.n: ‘brēat’ is the past of ‘brēotan’, ‘break, kill’, and ‘bolgenmōd’ ‘swollen-minded, enraged’ (‘bolgen’ the participle of ‘belgan’, ‘swell with anger’). ‘bēodgenēatas’ are ‘table-companions’ (‘bēod’ ‘table’ and ‘genēat’ ‘companion’), and ‘eaxlgesteallan’ ‘shoulder-companions’, an accusative plural of ‘eaxlgestealla’ (‘eaxl’ ‘shoulder’ and ‘gestealla’ ‘comrade’), the men who stood at his side. ‘oþ þæt hē āna hwearf’ is ‘until he went alone’, ‘hwearf’ the past of ‘hweorfan’, ‘turn, go away’. ‘mǣre þēoden’ is ‘the famed prince’, and ‘mondrēamum from’ is ‘away from the joys of men’: here ‘from’ is the preposition ‘fram’ placed after its noun, and not an adjective meaning ‘bold’.

sentences.t:
Ðēah þe hine mihtig God mægenes wynnum,
eafeþum stēpte, ofer ealle men
forð gefremede, hwæþere him on ferhþe grēow
brēosthord blōdrēow;
sentences.l: Although mighty God exalted him with the joys of might, with powers, advanced him forth over all men, yet in his spirit there grew a breast-hoard, blood-fierce;
sentences.i: Though mighty God had raised him up with the joys of strength and with powers, and set him forward above all men, yet there grew in his heart a bloodthirsty store of thoughts;
sentences.n: ‘Ðēah þe’ is ‘although’, and the two verbs ‘stēpte’ (‘raised up, exalted’, from ‘stēpan’) and ‘forð gefremede’ (‘advanced forth’) have ‘hine’ (Heremod) as object and ‘mihtig God’ as subject. ‘mægenes wynnum’ is ‘with the joys of might’, ‘eafeþum’ ‘with powers’, both datives. ‘hwæþere’ is ‘yet, nevertheless’, and the clause that follows has its own subject, ‘brēosthord’, ‘breast-hoard’: a hoard kept in the breast, so his thoughts and intents, a kenning like ‘wordhord’, ‘word-hoard’. ‘blōdrēow’ is ‘blood-fierce’ (‘rēow’ ‘fierce, raging’). So God’s favour is set against what grew in the man.

sentences.t:
nallas bēagas geaf
Denum æfter dōme;
sentences.l: not at all did he give rings to the Danes according to honour;
sentences.i: he gave no rings to the Danes as honour required;
sentences.n: ‘nallas’ is ‘not at all’, and ‘bēagas geaf’ ‘gave rings’, the generosity expected of a king who is a ‘bēaga brytta’, ‘dispenser of rings’ (so Hrothgar is called in Beowulf’s speech before the dive). ‘Denum’ is a dative plural, ‘to the Danes’. ‘æfter dōme’ is ‘according to honour’, so ‘as custom and honour demanded’, ‘dōm’ meaning ‘judgement, custom, glory’.

sentences.t:
drēamlēas gebād,
þæt hē þæs gewinnes weorc þrōwade,
lēodbealo longsum.
sentences.l: joyless he lived to see that he suffered the pain of that strife, a long people-bale.
sentences.i: Joyless, he lived on to suffer the pain of that strife, a long affliction to his people.
sentences.n: ‘drēamlēas’ is ‘joyless’ (‘drēam’ ‘joy’, as in ‘mondrēamum’ above). ‘gebād’ is the past of ‘gebīdan’, ‘live through, wait for’, and the ‘þæt’ clause says what he lived through: ‘þæt hē þæs gewinnes weorc þrōwade’ is ‘that he suffered the pain of that strife’, ‘weorc’ here ‘pain, toil’, ‘þrōwade’ the past of ‘þrōwian’, ‘suffer’. ‘lēodbealo longsum’ is ‘long-lasting people-bale’, in apposition, a calamity to the people; whether the ‘long’ is Heremod’s years of exile or the people’s sorrow the text does not say.

sentences.t:
Ðū þē lǣr be þon,
gumcyste ongit!
sentences.l: You, teach yourself from this; understand manly virtue!
sentences.i: Learn from this, and understand what makes a man good!
sentences.n: ‘Ðū’ is the stressed ‘you’ opening the lesson. ‘lǣr’ is the imperative of ‘lǣran’, ‘teach’, with the reflexive dative ‘þē’, so ‘teach yourself, learn’, and ‘be þon’ is ‘by that’, that is, by Heremod’s example. ‘ongit’ is the imperative of ‘ongietan’, ‘understand’. ‘gumcyste’ is the object, ‘manly virtue’ (‘guma’ ‘man’ and ‘cyst’ ‘excellence’), as in ‘gumcystum’ at 1486. Beowulf is told to learn the virtue Heremod lacked.

sentences.t:
Ic þis gid be þē
āwræc wintrum frōd.
sentences.l: I told this tale about you, wise with winters.
sentences.i: I have told this tale on your account, wise with many winters.
sentences.n: ‘gid’ is ‘speech, tale, song’, as at 1065. ‘āwræc’ is the past of ‘āwrecan’, ‘utter, recite’, with ‘be þē’ ‘about you’, and the subject is the stated ‘Ic’, Hrothgar. ‘wintrum frōd’ is ‘wise with winters’, a dative plural of manner, the phrase used of old and wise men.

sentences.t:
Wundor is tō secgan,
hū mihtig God manna cynne
þurh sīdne sefan snyttru bryttað,
eard ond eorlscipe;
sentences.l: It is a wonder to say how mighty God deals out wisdom to the race of men through a broad mind, land and noble rank;
sentences.i: It is a wonder to tell how mighty God, in his great mind, deals out wisdom to mankind, with land and noble rank;
sentences.n: ‘Wundor is tō secgan’ is ‘it is a wonder to say’. The manuscript has ‘secganne’, the inflected infinitive that usually follows ‘tō’; Klaeber prints ‘secgan’, changing the last letters (the italic ‘an’), and the apparatus refers to his textual notes § 12. The sense is the same. ‘hū … bryttað’ is the clause saying what is wonderful: ‘bryttað’ is the third person of ‘bryttian’, ‘deal out’, a verb of the ‘brytta’ who distributes rings. ‘manna cynne’ is a dative, ‘to the race of men’, ‘þurh sīdne sefan’ ‘through a wide mind’, so God’s large and generous mind, and ‘snyttru’ ‘wisdom’ the object, with ‘eard ond eorlscipe’ (‘land and noble rank’) added to it.

sentences.t: hē āh ealra geweald.
sentences.l: he owns power over all.
sentences.i: he has power over everything.
sentences.n: ‘āh’ is the third person of ‘āgan’, ‘own, possess’, and ‘ealra geweald’ ‘power of all’, ‘geweald’ the object and ‘ealra’ its genitive. The same claim is made of the Measurer at 1610.

sentences.t:
Hwīlum hē on lufan lǣteð hworfan
monnes mōdgeþonc mǣran cynnes,
seleð him on ēþle eorþan wynne
tō healdanne hlēoburh wera,
gedēð him swā gewealdẹne worolde dǣlas,
sīde rīce, þæt hē his selfa ne mæg
his unsnyttrum ende geþencean.
sentences.l: At times he lets the mind-thought of a man of famed kin turn in love, gives him in his homeland the joy of the earth to hold, a shelter-fortress of men, makes the parts of the world so subject to him, a wide realm, so that he himself in his folly cannot think out the end of it.
sentences.i: At times he lets the mind of a man of famous family turn in delight; he gives him joy of the land to hold in his own country, a stronghold of men; he makes the parts of the world so subject to him, a wide realm, that in his folly he cannot imagine the end of it.
sentences.n: ‘Hwīlum’ is ‘at times’, ‘at times’. ‘lǣteð hworfan’ is ‘lets turn’, a verb of letting with an infinitive, and ‘monnes mōdgeþonc mǣran cynnes’ is ‘the mind-thought of a man of famous kin’, ‘mǣran cynnes’ a genitive of quality. ‘on lufan’ is ‘in love’, so ‘in pleasure, with delight’; the apparatus lists Grein’s ‘on luste’, Holthausen’s ‘on luston’ and Sedgefield’s ‘on hlīsan’. ‘seleð him’ is ‘gives him’, ‘eorþan wynne’ ‘earth’s joy’, ‘tō healdanne’ an inflected infinitive, ‘to hold’, and ‘hlēoburh wera’ ‘shelter-fortress of men’ (‘hlēo’ ‘shelter’), a stronghold that protects its people. The apparatus reads the manuscript’s ‘ge deð’ (two words) in ‘gedēð’. ‘gewealdẹne’ is an accusative plural, ‘subject, under rule’, with ‘worolde dǣlas’ (‘parts of the world’) and ‘sīde rīce’ (‘wide realm’) in apposition; the dot under the ‘ẹ’ is the same metrical sign as before. In the last clause ‘his selfa’ (‘himself’) is the subject’s emphasis, ‘ende geþencean’ ‘think out the end’, and ‘his unsnyttrum’ ‘in his folly’; the genitive ‘his’ may mean ‘of it’. Thorkelin and Thorpe, among others, read ‘for his unsnyttrum’, ‘because of his folly’, and the manuscript has ‘his’; Trautmann reads ‘sēlþa’ for ‘selfa’. The grammar of this clause is uncertain; I follow the sense that the fortunate man cannot foresee a limit to his good fortune.

sentences.t: Wunað hē on wiste;
sentences.l: He dwells in plenty;
sentences.i: He lives in plenty;
sentences.n: ‘Wunað’ is the third person of ‘wunian’, ‘dwell, live’, and ‘on wiste’ ‘in abundance’, ‘wist’ meaning food and well-being. The semicolon begins a list of what does not touch him.

sentences.t:
nō hine wiht dweleð
ādl nē yldo, nē him inwitsorh
on sefa(n) sweorceð, nē gesacu ōhwǣr
ecghete ēoweð, ac him eal worold
wendeð on willan;
sentences.l: not at all does sickness or age hinder him, nor does malice-sorrow darken in his mind, nor does strife anywhere show sword-hate, but for him all the world turns to his will;
sentences.i: No sickness or age troubles him; no malicious grief clouds his mind; no strife shows the hatred of the sword anywhere; the whole world turns to suit his wish;
sentences.n: ‘nō hine wiht dweleð’ is ‘in no way does anything hinder him’, ‘dweleð’ the third person of ‘dwelian’, which the lexica give as ‘lead astray, hinder’; the subjects follow, ‘ādl nē yldo’ (‘sickness nor age’). ‘inwitsorh’ is ‘malice-sorrow’ (‘inwit’ ‘malice, evil design’ and ‘sorh’ ‘sorrow’), and ‘sweorceð’ the third person of ‘sweorcan’, ‘grow dark’. The parentheses in ‘sefa(n)’ mark a letter Klaeber restored: the manuscript reading is ‘sefa:’ in Zupitza’s edition and ‘sefad’ in the Thorkelin copies, and Grundtvig and Kemble print ‘sefan’, ‘in the mind’. ‘gesacu’ is ‘strife’, and ‘ecghete’ ‘sword-hate’; the apparatus lists Grein, Holthausen and Sedgefield, who read ‘gesaca’, ‘an adversary’, for ‘gesacu’. ‘ēoweð’ is ‘shows’, ‘ōhwǣr’ ‘anywhere’. ‘ac him eal worold wendeð on willan’ is ‘but for him all the world turns to his will’.

sentences.t: hē þæt wyrse ne con —,
sentences.l: he knows no worse.
sentences.i: he knows nothing worse —
sentences.n: ‘þæt wyrse’ is ‘the worse (thing)’, a neuter comparative used as a noun, and ‘con’ the third person of ‘cunnan’, ‘know’. The dash tells us Klaeber’s sentence is not finished: this part ends in the middle of the sentence, with the fortunate man still at the height of his fortune.
